result.markdown: --- title: "Lecture 11" from: markdown+emoji subtitle: "Final remarks and things we did not discuss..." format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: true logo: NTNU_UofG.png theme: uofg_theme.scss footer: "Back to Home" header-includes: | slide-number: "c/t" title-slide-attributes: # data-background-image: images/trondheim3.png data-background-size: cover data-background-opacity: "0.55" author: - name: Sara Martino #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: sara.martino@ntnu.no affiliations: Dept. of Mathematical Science, NTNU - name: Janine Illian #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: Janine.Illian@glasgow.ac.uk affiliations: University of Glasgow - name: Jafet Belmont #orcid: 0000-0002-6879-4412 email: Jafet.Belmont@glasgow.ac.uk affiliations: University of Glasgow # date: May 22, 2025 bibliography: ../references.bib embed-resources: true execute: allow-html: true freeze: auto --- ## What we have discusssed in this course{.smaller} - General principles of INLA and `inlabru` - Temporal Models - Spatial Models - Areal Data - Geostatistical Data - Point Processes - Spatio-temporal Models - Multi-likelihood Models - Comparing and Evaluating Models . . . INLA and `inlabru` are still evolving, a lot of other things are available (at different levels of maturity!) ## Other topics one could be interested in{.smaller} - Covariates with effect that changes in space and/or time - Observing aggregated quantities - Modeling non-stationarity - Barrier Model - Using covariates in the covariance structure - More complex spatial and spatio-temporal models - Non-separable spatio-temporal models - Fractional SPDE model - Modeling spatial dependences on different domains - Other - Distance sampling - Modeling Animal movement data - Self-exciting Hawks processes # Space/time varying covariate effects ## Space/time varying covariate effects ![](figures/varying_covariates.png){fig-align="center"} ## Space/time varying covariate effects The model $$ \eta(s) = \beta_0 + \beta_1(s)\ x(s) $$ Implementation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp = ~ Intercept(0) + space_beta(geometry, weights = covariate, model = spde) # OR cmp = ~ Intercept(0) + space_beta(idx_region, weights = covariate, model = "besag") ``` ::: ## Some relevant references - Vignette on the [inlabru website](https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/svc.html) ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@belmont2024spatio"} ::: # Observing aggregated quantities ## Observing aggregated quantities{.smaller} Sometimes we do not observe our quantity of interest directly . . . :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} We have emissions at NUTS2 level, want to downscale at NUTS3 - At NUTS3 (unobserved) - $y_i \sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_i,\sigma^2)$ - $\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i+u_i$ - At NUTS2 (observed data) - $Z_j = \sum_{i\in A_j}y_i\sim\mathcal{N}(m_j,\sigma^2_j)$ - $m_j = \sum_{i\in A_j}(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_i+u_i)$ and $\sigma^2_j\approx\frac{\sigma^2}{N_j} $ ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/aggregated0.png){width=100%} ::: :::: ## Observing aggregated quantities ![](figures/Aggregated1.png) ## Observing aggregated quantities Model set-up ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cmp <- ~ 0 + beta(1, prec.linear = 1) + space(main = space, model = "besag", graph = INLA::inla.matrix2graph(Q), scale.model = T) + covariate(cov, model= "linear") mapper1 <- bm_aggregate(rescale = FALSE,n_block = max(nuts3$block)) formula1 = y2 ~ ibm_eval(mapper1, input = list(block = block, weights = weight), state = beta + space + covariate) # Construct the likelihood lik1 <- bru_obs( formula = formula1, scale = 1/data_obs$n_reg, data = nuts3 , response_data = data_obs) ``` ::: ## Some notes and relevant references - The aggregation is easy if the likelihood is Gaussian - It is also easy for Poisson data (but need the non-linear approximation) - More complicated for other likelihood models :::{style="margin-top: 2em;"} ::: ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;".refs-subset data-keys="@lindgren2024inlabru @wu2026arealdisaggregationsmallarea @villejo2026spatiotemporalblockaggregationmodel "} ::: # Modeling non-stationarity ## The barrier model - Motivation Physical barriers (walls, islands, lakes...) have an effect on the phenomenon under study: ![](figures/barrier0.png) ## The barrier model - Define which mesh nodes are barrier and which are not - Two different ranges for the two regions types ![](figures/barrier1.png) ## The barrier model - Results ![](figures/barrier2.png) **Note** To make some difference the barrier has to be large enough (more than the range...) ## Barrier Model - some references ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@bakka2019non @panunzi2025estimating"} ::: ## Modeling non-stationarity in with covariates Sometimes we want the covariance to depends not only on the distance but also on the locations. . . . The SPDE apporach make it possible to use covariates in the covariance structure $$ \left(\kappa(s)^2-\Delta\right)\tau(s)u(s) = \mathcal{W}(s) $$ where we can have $$ \log\tau(s) = \theta_{\tau,1} + \sum_jb_{\tau,j}\theta_{\tau,j}, \qquad\log\kappa(s) = \theta_{\kappa,1} + \sum_jb_{\kappa,j}\theta_{\kappa,j}, $$ ## Modeling non-stationarity in space ![](figures/non-stationary1.png) ## Modeling non-stationarity in space - some references Note: A more flexible approach using basis functions instead of covariates is also possible :::{style = "margin-top: 2em;"} ::: ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@ingebrigtsen2014spatial @ingebrigtsen2015estimation @fuglstad2015exploring @fuglstad2015does"} ::: # More complex spatial and spatio-temporal models ## Non-separable spatio-temporal models All the space-time models we have seen are separable: $$ \text{Cov}\{x(\mathbf{s}_1,t_1),x(\mathbf{s}_2,t_2)\} = C_S(\mathbf{s}_1,\mathbf{s}_2)\, C_T(t_1,t_2). $$ - Spatial and temporal dependence act independently. - Implies that the temporal correlation structure is the same at all spatial scales. **Advantages** - Easy to specify and compute. - Easy to interpret **Disdvantages** - Can be unrealistic for physical processes where information propagates through space over time (examples: Weather systems moving across a region, Ocean currents, Air pollution transport, Spread of infectious diseases...) ## Non-separable spatio-temporal models In ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@Lindgren_Bakka_Bolin_Krainski_Rue_2024"} ::: a non-separable model for the space-time covariance: $$ \text{Cov}\{x(\mathbf{s}_1,t_1),x(\mathbf{s}_2,t_2)\}, $$ is defined through a diffusion equation. What they get: - Spatial dependence is represented by a Matérn field. - Temporal evolution is driven by a diffusion process. - Information can spread across space as time passes. - This naturally induces a **non-separable** covariance structure. [GitHub repo](https://eliaskrainski.github.io/INLAspacetime/) for the project ## Fractional SPDE models The "basic" SPDE approach solved equations of the kind: $$ (κ^2−Δ)^βu=𝒲. $$ for integer values of $2\beta$ and $\beta$ fixed. . . . The `rSPDE` package provides efficient approximations when β is a general fractional power. As a result, one can easily do inference and prediction using fractional SPDE models such as $$ (κ^2−Δ)^βu=𝒲. $$ In particular, it allows for bayesian inference of all model parameters, including the fractional parameter β. ## Fractional SPDE models ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@Fractional1 @Fractional2"} ::: :::{style = "margin-top:2em;"} ::: For more info see the [github repo for this project](https://davidbolin.github.io/rSPDE/) # Modeling spatial dependences on different domains ## Metric Graph - Not all phenomena leave on $\mathcal{R}^2$ - Example: Traffic on roads, fishes in a river, etc... ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](figures/metric_graph1.png) ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](figures/metric_graph2.png) ::: ::::: . . . - What is different from $\mathcal{R}^2$? ## Metric Graph - What is different from $\mathcal{R}^2$? - Think about distances on the road network...they often do not correspond to the euclidian distance in $\mathcal{R}^2$ - The random walk has to account for the shape of the graph - ..this is what the [MetricGraph library](https://davidbolin.github.io/MetricGraph/index.html) does :::{style = "margin-top:2em;"} ::: ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@lilleborge2025joint @recachobayesian @bolin2026log"} ::: ..and many more papers from the group of David Bolin # Other ## Distance Sampling - Complex observation models {.smaller auto-animate="true" background-color="#FFFFFF"} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: - Standard distance sampling approaches specify $g(s)$ as a function that declines with increasing distance - perpendicular distance to the transect line for *line transects* ![](figures/whale_watch.png){fig-align="center" width="398"} ## Thinned Point Process {.smaller} ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: - flexible approach that can include spatial covariates to model the mean intensity and a spatially structured random effect to account for unexplained heterogeneity not captured by the covariates. - to account for the imperfect detection of points we specify a thinning probability function $$ g(s) = \text{Prob}(\text{a point at s is detected}|\text{a point is at s}) $$ - key property -- an LGCP with intensity $\lambda(s)$ that thinned by a probability function $g(s)$, follows also a LGCP with intensity: $$ \underbrace{\tilde{\lambda}(s)}_{\text{observed process}} = \underbrace{\lambda(s)}_{\text{true process}} \times \underbrace{g(s)}_{\text{thinning probability}} $$ ## Some revant papers about distance sampling Tutorial on the [`inlabru` github](https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_distancesampling.html) :::{style = "margin-top:2em;"} ::: ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@martino2021integration"} ::: ## Modelling movement data - models can also be fitted to movement data in `inlabru` - sometimes locations treated as a point pattern, ignoring sequential nature of the data - model development is an area of active research - approaches include: - discrete time step-selection processes and - continuous time Langevin diffusion models ![](figures/movement.png){fig-align="center"} ## Some relevant papers about animal movement :::{style = "margin-top:2em;"} ::: ::: {style = "font-size: 0.7em;" .refs-subset data-keys="@arce2023accounting @megan_thesis"} ::: ## Self exciting Hawks Processes{.smaller} A self-exciting process is a point process in which the occurrence of an event increases the probability of further events occurring shortly afterwards. $$ \lambda(t) = \mu + \sum_{t_i // 1. link each full-list entry to references.html (your existing code) document.querySelectorAll('#refs [id^="ref-"]').forEach(function(entry) { var a = document.createElement('a'); a.href = '../references.html#' + entry.id; a.target = '_blank'; a.style.textDecoration = 'none'; a.style.color = 'inherit'; while (entry.firstChild) a.appendChild(entry.firstChild); entry.appendChild(a); }); // 2. copy chosen entries into each .refs-subset slide var refs = document.getElementById('refs'); document.querySelectorAll('.refs-subset').forEach(function(box) { box.className += ' ' + refs.className; box.dataset.keys.split(/[\s,;]+/).forEach(function(k) { k = k.replace(/^@/, ''); if (!k) return; var src = document.getElementById('ref-' + k); if (!src) { console.warn('refs-subset: no entry for ' + k); return; } var copy = src.cloneNode(true); copy.removeAttribute('id'); box.appendChild(copy); }); }); ```

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
